Fairway bunkers, bigger. Powder bunkers out in the fairways are now about half as big again as round 2's (up to 36 × 21 m), and a long one can follow a fairway's edge. Greenside black-sand bunkers stay their size. This is now a rule for every course.

1, The Ice Gate. A long powder bunker runs down the left of the landing area, about 200–335 m from the back tee and 130 m long, a few metres of rough off the fairway's left edge. Its edge swells and pinches like a fairway's. The boulders now sit past it.

3, The Longship. The lead across the carry is gone. In its place, a hole of open black water in the ice short of the green, about 20 m before its front and 37 m across, ragged at the edge. A shot that would have skated up to the shore can run into it if it's topped or thin. The Hare tee's line to the left shore stays dry.

5, The Seracs. A pod of short grass right of the green, so a ball off the long bench has a way in. Two powder bunkers bite into the bench's right edge (about 170–225 m out) and a small one sits short left of the green. Five shorter seracs, 7–10 m tall, now stand either side of the approach, 230–250 m out: a drive through the gap that comes up short can still clip one.

6, The Frozen Falls. The shelf is now the broken edge of an ice sheet, 15 m high: a craggy face that wanders in bays and prows right across the view, with a raised, broken crest and seracs leaning off its lip. In the middle the falls build out from the face in a bulge of ropey columns of ice that run from the lip to the ground and flare where they land, with icicles hanging free at their edges and here and there along the lip. A skirt of ice spreads out at the foot, with broken ice along the rest of the face. A long black-sand bunker wraps the green from its front left round the back.

Still open. Powder needs its own lie when the course is built in the game (it plays as sand on the plan's drives). The longship, the mammoth, the hall and the ice cave are drawn as plan shapes only until the art pass.
